Basis: the owner's right to enjoy and dispose of his property (civil code, ownership chapter, art. 674) and the rule that no one is deprived of his property except as the law provides (art. 677); check the paragraph that carries the right to recover the thing from whoever holds it without right.

Element 1: the plaintiff's ownership of the property, proven by a published (registered) title deed; check the rule that real rights are not transferred, even between the parties, without publication at the land registry (civil code art. 793 and ordinance 75-74).
Element 2: the defendant's actual occupation of the property, and its date; usually proven by a bailiff's record of findings (محضر معاينة).

Element 3: the absence of any title in the occupier (no lease, loan for use, sale promise, co-ownership share, family right); check who bears the proof of the negative fact and whether the occupier must prove the title he alleges (proof rules: the plaintiff proves his right, the debtor proves his release).
Burden of proof: the owner proves ownership and occupation; the occupier who pleads a lease or other title must prove it; check writing requirements for proving a lease.

Competent section: the real-estate section of the court (CPCA articles on the real-estate section); also check whether the urgent-matters judge (référé) may order eviction of an occupier without title as a measure that does not touch the merits.
Territorial jurisdiction: the court where the property lies, for claims about real property (CPCA art. 40); check whether that rule is of public order.

Exit from the ordinary courts: if a party is the State, a wilaya, a commune or a public administrative body, or the property is public domain, the administrative court may be competent (CPCA art. 800-801).
Exit: if the occupation was obtained by a criminal act (trespass on property, art. 386 penal code), check whether a criminal case on the same facts suspends the civil claim.

Time limit for the eviction claim itself: the ownership claim (revendication) is not lost by lapse of time, but check acquisitive prescription by the occupier (15 years of possession, civil code art. 827; 10 years with just title and good faith, art. 828) as a defence.

Time limit for damages: tort action is barred 15 years from the harmful act (civil code art. 133); check whether the occupation is a continuing act and how the period counts; limitation is raised only on a plea, not by the court of its own motion.

Damages for occupation without right: civil code art. 124 (fault, harm, causation); also check the rules on the possessor in bad faith returning fruits (civil code art. 837-839) as an alternative ground for an occupation indemnity.

Formal notice: check whether a formal notice is required before claiming damages; civil code art. 181 says no notice is needed when the obligation is compensation for a harmful act; check whether a notice to leave is required before the eviction claim (probably not a condition of admissibility).

Land registry publication of the petition: CPCA art. 17 requires publication of a petition concerning published real property or a real right; check whether a pure eviction claim falls within it, and the sanction (inadmissibility, publication proof at the first hearing).

Petition formal elements: CPCA art. 15 (court, parties' names and domiciles, facts, requests, grounds, documents), art. 8 Arabic language and official translation, fees, standing and interest (art. 13).

Possessory actions boundary: a claim to protect possession (recovery of possession, stopping disturbance) must be filed within one year of the disturbance (CPCA art. 524 and following); it is not the owner's eviction claim; check that possessory and ownership claims cannot be combined (non-cumul).
Boundary: an occupier holding over after a lease ends is a former tenant: lease rules (civil code art. 467 and following, notice to quit, art. 469 bis) apply, not this claim.
Boundary: a commercial tenant (commercial code art. 172 and following) has eviction-compensation rights; an eviction claim against him follows the commercial lease regime.
Boundary: a co-owner in undivided ownership is not an occupier without title; the remedy is partition or the rules on co-ownership management.
Boundary: an occupier who built or planted on the land: check the rules on buildings by a third party on another's land (civil code art. 784-786) and the owner's choice to keep or demolish.
Boundary: an occupier with a family right (a former spouse with custody keeping the marital home) falls under the family code.
Requests: eviction of the defendant and anyone occupying through him; damages (occupation indemnity) with an amount; accessory requests: provisional execution, penalty payment (astreinte), costs.

Documents: published title deed or certificate of ownership/land book; bailiff's record of findings of occupation; notice to leave and its proof of service, if any; cadastral plan or property description.
Check amendments: CPCA (law 08-09) as amended by law 22-13 (specialised commercial courts, conciliation); civil code art. 124 as amended by law 05-10.
Check the rule on the defendant's domicile unknown (service by publication) and the defendant residing abroad (periods extended).
